blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Post-training quantisation reduces the memory cost of large language models, but it remains unclear whether compression preserves language skills of regional varieties as reliably as their standard-language counterparts. We study this question for Bavarian, Standard German, and English using BAVGROUND, a multiple-choice benchmark, where 206 source questions are aligned across all three languages. Across 14 open-weight 7B--10B instruction models, we compare BF16 with 8-bit GPTQ and two 4-bit settings, GPTQ and AWQ. Eight-bit GPTQ remains close to BF16 and largely preserves the relative behaviour of the three languages, while 4-bit quantisation was found to be much less stable. The two 4-bit methods reduce average accuracy by about 1.4--1.5 percentage points and change 11.9--16.0% of BF16 decisions, with changes concentrated on examples where the BF16 model is already uncertain. This instability does not translate into a consistent Bavarian disadvantage. Although Bavarian, a low-resource dialect, has lower baseline accuracy than German and English, the language most affected at 4 bits varies across models and quantisation methods. Calibration further shapes these cross-language effects: the relative Bavarian--German effect changes with calibration language, while changing the calibration source has little average effect on GPTQ-4 but can affect AWQ-4 much more strongly. Free-form evaluation on five models further shows that 4-bit compression can degrade generated responses even in settings where multiple-choice accuracy changes only modestly, while 8-bit GPTQ remains comparatively stable. Overall, our results show that quantisation robustness for regional language varieties depends on the model, quantisation method, calibration data, and evaluation setting, and cannot be measured by aggregate multilingual accuracy alone.
blocks.zh: 训练后量化降低了大型语言模型的内存成本,但目前仍不清楚压缩能否像标准语言的对应物那样可靠地保留了区域品种的语言技能. 我们用BAVGROUND这一多选择基准来研究巴伐利亚语、标准德语和英语的这个问题,在这三种语言中,206个源问题都一致。 跨越14个开口重的7B-10B指令模型,我们比较了BF16和8位GPTQ以及两个4位设置,GPTQ和AWQ. 八位GPTQ仍然与BF16相近,并基本保持了三种语言的相对行为,而4位的四位分解则被认为稳定得多. 两种4位法将平均精度降低约1.4-1.5个百分点并更改了11.9-16.0%的BF16决定,而改变集中于BF16模型已经不确定的例子. 这种不稳定并没有转化为巴伐利亚一贯的劣势. 虽然低资源方言巴伐利亚语的基线精度低于德语和英语,但以4比特受影响最大的语言在模型和量化方法上有所不同. 校正进一步塑造了这些跨语言效应:相对的巴伐利亚-德意志效应会用校正语言来改变,而改变校正源对GPTQ-4几乎没有平均影响,但可以更强烈地影响AWQ-4. 对5个模型的自由式评价进一步显示,4位压缩即使在多选择精度变化不大的环境下也能降解生成的响应,而8位的GPTQ仍然相对稳定. 总的来说,我们的结果表明,区域语言品种的量化稳健性取决于模型、量化方法、校准数据和评价设置,不能仅用多语种总体准确性来衡量。

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Post-training quantisation is increasingly used to reduce the memory cost of
large language models and enable deployment under tighter hardware budgets.
Weight-only methods such as GPTQ ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) and AWQ ( Lin et al., 2024 ) can substantially reduce model size while often preserving
aggregate benchmark accuracy. This makes quantisation particularly attractive
for open-weight models and deployment settings in which memory capacity is a
primary constraint.

However, preservation of aggregate performance does not imply that all
languages are preserved equally well. Multilingual models are trained and
evaluated disproportionately on high-resource standard languages, while
regional and low-resource varieties often receive less representation in

has shown that quantisation can affect languages unevenly and that automatic
metrics can underestimate degradation visible in generated outputs ( Marchisio et al., 2024 ) . What remains less understood is
whether these effects also extend to regional varieties that are
linguistically close to a high-resource standard language.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) ( Frantar et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ) converts the
weights and, in some approaches, the activations of a neural network from
their original 32- or 16-bit floating-point representations to lower-precision
formats, typically 8-bit or 4-bit integers. GPTQ uses approximate second-order
information to minimise layer-wise reconstruction error during low-bit weight
quantisation ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) , whereas AWQ identifies
activation-salient channels and rescales them prior to weight quantisation ( Lin et al., 2024 ) . These methods can provide strong quality–efficiency
trade-offs, with prior evaluations showing that moderate quantisation often
preserves much of a model’s aggregate performance, particularly for larger
models ( Giagnorio et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en:
Early studies established that neural networks can retain useful
performance under reduced numerical precision, while highlighting
their sensitivity to quantisation ( Sung et al., 2015 ) .
Aggregate performance, however, does not always change uniformly with
precision. Quantised models can sometimes match or even slightly outperform
their higher-precision counterparts on particular tasks or benchmarks ( Badshah and Sajjad, 2024 ; Lee et al., 2025 ) . Such improvements tend to
depend on the model, task, and evaluation setting rather than reflecting a
general benefit of lower precision. More importantly, stable or improved
aggregate scores can conceal losses on particular subsets of the evaluation
data. This makes it necessary to examine systematically where quantisation changes model
behaviour rather than treating aggregate robustness as evidence that all
capabilities are preserved equally.

blocks.en:
Recent work has examined these effects more directly in multilingual settings. Marchisio et al. (2024) show that quantisation
robustness varies substantially across languages and that automatic metrics
can miss degradation visible in generated outputs. Calibration data can also
shape these effects. Zeng et al. (2024) show that
multilingual calibration can improve preservation of lower-resource
languages, while Chimoto et al. (2026) find that the language
composition of GPTQ and AWQ calibration data affects multilingual
quantisation quality. These studies establish that language-specific
robustness depends on more than bit width alone. However, they primarily
compare distinct languages, where differences in script, typology, content,
and benchmark construction can accompany language identity. This leaves open
whether similar effects arise between a regional variety and its closely
related standard language when the underlying content is held fixed.

Accomplishing regional and cultural evaluation requires targeted benchmark datasets that can distinguish
language-specific effects from differences in the evaluated content. This is
particularly challenging for regional and culturally specific language
varieties, which are often unevenly represented in both training data and
existing benchmarks.
Evaluation of dialectal language skills receives increasing attention in the context of assessing Large language model (LLM) fairness and bias ( Lin et al., 2025 ) .
Often, the focus of these studies is on English, involving synthetically generated data and human-in-the loop validation, e.g. by Ziems et al. (2023) , but there are examples involving LLM-as-judge approaches too ( Faisal et al., 2025 ) .
LLMs have been shown to encode cultural
knowledge unevenly across regions and languages ( Santy et al., 2023 ; Arora et al., 2023 ) , while
reliably evaluating such knowledge remains an open problem ( Hershcovich et al., 2022 ) . Li et al. (2024) propose a method for incorporating cultural differences
into LLMs, while Durmus et al. (2024) investigate how language models represent subjective
opinions across countries.

blocks.en: 3 Experimental Setup
blocks.zh: 3 实验设置

blocks.en:

its own BF16 baseline. The three-way alignment of BavGround allows us to
measure performance changes on the same underlying questions in English,
Standard German, and Bavarian. We additionally measure peak GPU memory and
batch-size-one throughput on a single NVIDIA GH200 GPU. Full hardware and
runtime details are provided in Appendix B .

blocks.en: 3.1 Benchmark
blocks.zh: 3.1 基准

blocks.en:
Our work uses the BavGround dataset that contains 206 source questions, each realised in English, German
and Bavarian, yielding alltogether 618 multiple-choice instances. The questions of this dataset span eight
cultural domains which are each divided into two subsets: gen , covering broadly accessible (or general)
cultural knowledge, and grd , which consists of question-answer pairs hand-made constructed from regional newspapers,
historical references, and specialist anthropological sources. The evaluated set contains
240 gen and 378 grd instances. Because all three language versions correspond to the same source question,
cross-language comparisons are paired by source item rather than across
independent monolingual benchmarks.

blocks.en:
We evaluate 14 open-weight 7B–10B instruction models chosen to cover a range
of language and pretraining profiles. The main panel includes the
Bavarian-adapted GENBA-10B ( Hoffmann et al., 2025 ) , the German-focused LeoLM and LLaMmlein, five
European multilingual models (EuroLLM, Mistral, Occiglot, Teuken, and
Salamandra), and six broader multilingual models (Llama 3.1, Qwen2.5,
Gemma 2, Aya Expanse, Granite 3.0, and OLMo 2). GENBA-10B is specifically
adapted to English, German, and Bavarian, while Llama 3.1 provides a closely
related parent-model comparison. Exact checkpoint identifiers are listed in
Appendix C .

blocks.en: 3.3 Evaluation Protocol

blocks.en:
Our primary evaluation uses multiple-choice accuracy. For each question, we
select the answer candidate with the highest mean token-level conditional
log-likelihood given the question context. Length normalisation reduces
answer-length effects, while scoring the option text rather than A – D labels avoids model-specific label priors. We also
evaluate answer-letter likelihood and greedy generation as diagnostics for
label bias and output-format failures, but neither contributes to the primary
accuracy measure. We additionally evaluate free-form generation on five representative models
using all 618 BavGround instances. Each quantised response is compared
with its BF16 counterpart by a blinded pairwise LLM judge
( gpt-5.6-luna ). Judging prioritises semantic correctness, allows
ties, and considers Bavarian dialect appropriateness secondarily. A random
20% subset is repeated with reversed response order to check position bias.
Full judge instructions and coverage statistics are given in
Appendix A.14 .

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We asked whether making language models lighter through post-training
quantisation also preserves their behaviour across Bavarian, Standard German,
and English. For GPTQ-8, the answer is largely yes. Performance remains close
to BF16 and the relative differences between the three languages are broadly
preserved. At 4 bits, this stability weakens. Bavarian is not consistently
more affected than German, but the relative behaviour of the two languages
varies more across models, quantisation methods, and calibration data. The aligned dialect vs. standard language comparison is important here because these
changes are difficult to identify from aggregate multilingual accuracy
alone. It also shows that lower baseline performance in Bavarian does not by
itself imply greater fragility, while free-form evaluation reveals losses that
fixed-choice accuracy can miss. Our matrix of experiments indicates that quantisation can therefore make models
substantially lighter without necessarily harming Bavarian more than German,
but linguistic preservation at 4 bits cannot be assumed from compression
level alone. For regional language varieties, lightweight deployment and
linguistic robustness need to be evaluated together.

blocks.en: 7 Limitations
blocks.zh: 7 限制

blocks.en:
Our study focuses on Bavarian and BavGround , so the findings may not
generalise to other dialects or low-resource languages, and we do not model
Bavarian’s internal regional or orthographic variation. The free-form analysis broadens the evaluation beyond multiple choice but relies on a single LLM judge. The response-order audit shows high consistency, out of 9,270 planned
comparisons, 112 were excluded due to output truncation and 14 due
to malformed pair identifiers. The calibration-language ablation is deliberately focused, covering four
models and one seed per condition. The calibration-source experiment adds three-seed replication for the
focused four-model comparison while its broader seed-42 comparison uses
balanced calibration, with 14 valid GPTQ-4 and 13 valid AWQ-4 pairs.
Broader replication would therefore be useful for establishing how stable
these calibration effects are across models and seeds. Finally, the memory results are specific to our hardware, software stack, and
batch-size-one inference setup.
